title: DeepMind's FunSearch produces a cap set of size 512 in dimension 8 and raises the asymptotic lower bound on the size of cap sets
summary: DeepMind's FunSearch, which pairs a large language model with an automated evaluator, produced a cap set of size 512 in dimension 8 and raised the asymptotic lower bound for cap sets to 2.2202.
account: On 14 December 2023 Nature published a paper by Google DeepMind researchers with mathematician Jordan Ellenberg (University of Wisconsin–Madison) that describes FunSearch. FunSearch pairs a pretrained large language model that proposes programs with an automated evaluator that scores them, in an island-based evolutionary loop. Applied to the cap set problem, FunSearch produced a program that generates a cap set of size 512 in dimension 8, exceeding the previous best known construction of 496. Ellenberg exploited a symmetry that he noticed in the program's output. FunSearch then found admissible sets that raised the asymptotic lower bound from 2.2180 to 2.2202. The same day, Terence Tao told MIT Technology Review that the approach is a promising paradigm. In a comment dated 11 January 2024, Ernest Davis of New York University, who was not an author, accepted that the constructions are genuine and rated their mathematical importance as moderate. In a survey posted on 5 August 2024, the cap set specialists Ernie Croot, Vsevolod Lev and Péter Pál Pach list the FunSearch bound of 2.2202 as one step in the record. They also cite an unpublished manuscript by Naslund that claims 2.2208. On 11 August 2025 Zhai and colleagues described X-evolve, a method powered by large language models, in an arXiv preprint. In a preprint of 18 June 2026, Paul Hametner and Fred Tyrrell credit FunSearch with the first AI-assisted improvement and give 2.2203, from X-evolve, as the current record.
purpose: Built to search program space for constructions and heuristics in mathematics and computer science. The cap set constructions were that purpose.
system: FunSearch using Codey, a PaLM 2-based code model, with an evolutionary search and automated evaluator
deployer: DeepMind with Jordan Ellenberg (University of Wisconsin–Madison)
segment: Industrial research laboratory with academic collaborator

ratings.reason: Mathematicians gained an explicit cap set of size 512 in dimension 8 and an improved asymptotic bound. Davis, who was not an author, judged that the results are moderately interesting mathematically.

ai_role.statement: FunSearch generated the programs whose outputs are the cap sets and admissible sets. These are explicit finite objects that the evaluator and readers can verify mechanically. The 2.2202 bound depended on a human (Ellenberg) noticing a symmetry in FunSearch's output and refocusing the search. Davis identifies that as the most notable aspect.

display.answer: The Nature paper is the makers' own account, and the MIT Technology Review report of the same day quotes Terence Tao. Ernest Davis, Croot and colleagues, Zhai and colleagues, and Hametner and Tyrrell are not FunSearch authors. Tyrrell developed the admissible-set framework that FunSearch used, and Croot and colleagues and Hametner and Tyrrell cite the Nature paper for the FunSearch bound.
The geopolitical implications are unclear.

fields.summary: DeepMind's FunSearch, which pairs a large language model with an automated evaluator, produced a cap set of size 512 in dimension 8 and raised the asymptotic lower bound for cap sets to 2.2202.
fields.account: On 14 December 2023 Nature published a paper by Google DeepMind researchers with mathematician Jordan Ellenberg (University of Wisconsin–Madison) that describes FunSearch. FunSearch pairs a pretrained large language model that proposes programs with an automated evaluator that scores them, in an island-based evolutionary loop. Applied to the cap set problem, FunSearch produced a program that generates a cap set of size 512 in dimension 8, exceeding the previous best known construction of 496. Ellenberg exploited a symmetry that he noticed in the program's output. FunSearch then found admissible sets that raised the asymptotic lower bound from 2.2180 to 2.2202. The same day, Terence Tao told MIT Technology Review that the approach is a promising paradigm. In a comment dated 11 January 2024, Ernest Davis of New York University, who was not an author, accepted that the constructions are genuine and rated their mathematical importance as moderate. In a survey posted on 5 August 2024, the cap set specialists Ernie Croot, Vsevolod Lev and Péter Pál Pach list the FunSearch bound of 2.2202 as one step in the record. They also cite an unpublished manuscript by Naslund that claims 2.2208. On 11 August 2025 Zhai and colleagues described X-evolve, a method powered by large language models, in an arXiv preprint. In a preprint of 18 June 2026, Paul Hametner and Fred Tyrrell credit FunSearch with the first AI-assisted improvement and give 2.2203, from X-evolve, as the current record.

value.text: FunSearch generated and tested programs automatically within the researchers’ specification. A separate evaluator rejected invalid results.
